title: Psalm 78: Tell the Next Generation
summary: Asaph retells Israel's history as a lesson for the next generation, from the wonders in Egypt and the wilderness through the settlement in the land. Again and again the people forgot God's works, tested him, and rebelled, and again and again he judged them and showed mercy. The psalm ends with God rejecting the tent of Joseph and Shiloh and choosing Judah, Mount Zion, and David the shepherd king.
story: Psalm 78 is the second longest psalm (after Psalm 119) and the first of several historical psalms that retell Israel's story (compare Psalms 105, 106, and 136). It follows naturally from Psalm 77, which ended with God leading his people through the sea by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Psalm 78 picks up that story and carries it to David. In the setting of Book III, which wrestles with the loss of the temple and the failure of the monarchy, the psalm is a sober reminder that Israel's troubles have a long history of unfaithfulness behind them, and that God's choice of Zion and David was an act of grace to a people who didn't deserve it.
historical:
The heading reads “A Maskil of Asaph.” For Maskil and for Asaph and his guild, see Psalms 73 and 74. The psalm's date is debated. It ends with David shepherding Israel and says nothing about the division of the kingdom or the fall of Jerusalem, which leads some scholars to date it to the united monarchy under David or Solomon. Others point to its sharp contrast between rejected Ephraim (the leading northern tribe) and chosen Judah, and place it after the fall of the northern kingdom to Assyria in 722 BC, perhaps in Hezekiah's reign, when Judah was urging northern survivors to return to worship in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30). Still others date it later still.

The events it recounts are drawn from the books of Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, and 1 Samuel. Zoan (verses 12 and 43) was a city in the eastern Nile Delta, known to the Greeks as Tanis. The retreat of Ephraim's archers (verse 9) doesn't match any single event recorded elsewhere, and interpreters take it either as an unrecorded battle or as a picture of Ephraim's general failure. The abandonment of Shiloh (verse 60) refers to the period described in 1 Samuel 4, when the Philistines defeated Israel and captured the ark of the covenant; Shiloh, where the tabernacle had stood, was apparently destroyed around that time (compare Jeremiah 7:12-14).
cultural:
Israel was commanded to teach its children the story of what God had done (Deuteronomy 6:20-25), and Psalm 78 is itself an example of that practice. The father was expected to explain the meaning of festivals, laws, and memorials to his children. The psalm's opening, with its call to listen to instruction, sounds like a wisdom teacher addressing students, and it combines history with moral instruction.

Many details assume a reader who knows the wilderness stories: manna, the daily bread from heaven; the quail that came on the wind (Numbers 11:31-34), where the people died while the meat was still in their mouths; water from the rock (Exodus 17; Numbers 20). The plagues listed in verses 44 to 51 are fewer than the ten in Exodus and appear in a different order, showing that the psalm is selecting and arranging the events poetically. High places (verse 58) were local hilltop shrines, often associated with idol worship. The image of David taken from the sheepfolds (verse 70) draws on the widespread ancient picture of the king as shepherd of his people.
literary: Verses 1 to 8 form a prologue that states the psalm's purpose: to teach the next generation so that it will not repeat its fathers' failures. The history then unfolds in two long cycles. The first (verses 9 to 39) runs from Egypt through the wilderness: God's wonders, the people's rebellion, God's anger, and his compassion. The second (verses 40 to 72) begins again with the plagues in Egypt and moves through the exodus and settlement to the loss of Shiloh and the choice of Zion and David. Each cycle follows the pattern of grace, sin, judgment, and renewed mercy. Key words recur throughout: forget and remember, test and rebel, believe and not believe. The psalm ends not with Israel's failure but with God's choice of a shepherd.

outline.t: Ephraim forgot the wonders of Egypt and the wilderness
Testing God in the desert: manna and meat
The plagues, the exodus, and the land
Idolatry in the land and the loss of Shiloh
God chooses Judah, Zion, and David

doctrines.note: The psalm portrays sin as forgetting God's works, testing him, and failing to trust his salvation. Israel's history is a pattern of short-lived repentance followed by renewed rebellion, which shows how deep the human problem runs.

God's grace runs through the whole history: he provides water, manna, meat, guidance, and a land, and he is patient with a rebellious people. Verse 38 says he forgave their iniquity and often restrained his anger.
The prologue commands each generation to tell God's works to the next. Faith is handed down through teaching within families and communities, so that children put their confidence in God.
Israel's failure is described as unfaithfulness to God's covenant (verses 10 and 37). The psalm ends with God's choice of David, pointing to the covenant he made with David's house (2 Samuel 7).

words.note: Mashal, a proverb, parable, or comparison. In verse 2 it describes a saying that teaches by drawing lessons. Here the whole history of Israel becomes a mashal, a story whose pattern reveals truth for the next generation.
Chidah, a riddle or dark saying. In verse 2 it is paired with mashal. The things hidden from the beginning are not secrets but lessons in Israel's history that must be drawn out and understood.

Nasah, to test. Israel tested God in the wilderness (verses 18, 41, 56) by demanding proof of his power instead of trusting him. The same word describes God testing his people, but when people test God it is a sign of unbelief.

Bachar, to choose. In verses 67 to 70 God rejects Ephraim but chooses Judah, Mount Zion, and David. The choice is an act of grace, not reward, since the psalm has just shown that no tribe deserved it.

christ: Matthew quotes verse 2 to explain why Jesus taught in parables, saying this fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet (Matthew 13:34-35). Jesus spoke in parables that revealed things hidden since the foundation of the world. The manna, the bread of angels in verse 25, becomes the background for Jesus' teaching that he is the true bread from heaven (John 6:31-35). Paul uses the wilderness rebellion as a warning to the church (1 Corinthians 10:1-11), and says the rock that gave water was Christ. The psalm's final picture of David, the shepherd taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd God's people, looks ahead to Jesus, the son of David and the good shepherd (John 10:11).

hard.q: How can the psalm say that the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a warrior overcome by wine?
hard.a: Verse 65 uses a bold image. The Old Testament elsewhere says God never sleeps (Psalm 121:4), so the verse is not describing his nature but how events looked from Israel's side. After the disaster at Shiloh, when the ark was captured and God seemed inactive, the turn of events under Samuel, Saul, and David felt like God rousing himself to action. The comparison to a warrior shaking off wine is not a moral statement but a picture of sudden, overwhelming strength after apparent inactivity. Interpreters differ on the exact sense of the Hebrew (some take it as a warrior shouting from wine), but most agree it is poetic language describing God's intervention, similar to the prayers asking God to awake in Psalm 44:23.

questions: The psalm is written so that the next generation won't repeat its fathers' mistakes. What stories of God's faithfulness do you want to pass on?
Israel kept forgetting what God had done. What helps you remember God's past faithfulness when you face new trouble?
Verses 36 and 37 describe repentance that was only in words. How can you tell the difference between real repentance and words that don't last?
